description_en: The opening of the first movement of the B♭ major sinfonia, which also served as the overture to the opera Lucio Silla. The full orchestra throws the door open with force, and loud and soft passages trade places in quick succession. Two performances hold the climax back, while **only one reaches its climax within the first 30 seconds**.

The first two minutes or so of the chorus that opens the Magnificat. The orchestra opens forcefully in D major, and the chorus sings the first phrase, “Magnificat anima mea.” In all three performances the final chord is the loudest, and they differ in **how long they sustain loud playing before it**.

The lament of Orfeo, who has lost Euridice a second time by looking back. The same major-key melody returns three times, and twice the calling of her name breaks in, changing the key and the tempo. All three performances follow the same course, and they differ in **the loudness of the first sound**.

The complete overture, which Rossini opens with a snare-drum roll. After a march-like introduction, the fast main section brings two Rossini crescendos, built by repeating the same phrase and adding instruments one by one. Performances differ in **how much of the loud playing they hold in reserve**.

The opening of the fourth movement, in which an artist who has killed his beloved in a dream is led to the guillotine. After soft timpani rolls and off-beat horns, cellos and double basses present a descending minor-key theme. The theme grows as it passes from instrument to instrument, and **how softly the first timpani roll is played** is where the three performances differ most.

Johann Stamitz, a leading figure of the Mannheim school, opens his Clarinet Concerto with the tutti presenting the B♭ major theme; the solo clarinet then enters and takes up the song. In all three performances the music dips to its quietest at the same spot, and they differ in **where they place the loudest sound**.

The opening of the viola concerto that Henri Casadesus wrote under the name of J.C. Bach. The string tutti sets out the C minor theme with force, and then the solo viola enters. Performances differ in **how they carry the dynamic level on after the first tutti**.

Berlioz's orchestration of the Hungarian Rákóczi March. It opens with a soft wind signal, and the march theme swells several times; later, a long crescendo builds from a very soft passage and bursts into the full orchestra. Performances differ on **whether the loudest sound comes at the peak of the crescendo or at the very end**.

Glinka's song depicting a lark singing between sky and earth. After a piano prelude the voice sings the first verse, the piano carries on briefly, and the second verse returns with the same melody. The three performances differ on **whether the first or the second verse is sung loudest**.

An overture Berlioz built from melodies of his opera Benvenuto Cellini. After a short, explosive introduction, the English horn sings a long, slow love song; once it has passed to other instruments, the fast dance, a saltarello, drives on to the end. **The point at which the dance reaches nearly full volume** differs by more than two minutes between performances.

The two themes that open Scheherazade come one after the other. Brass and low strings sound the Sultan's theme loudly; after the woodwind chords die down, the solo violin unfolds Scheherazade's theme over the harp. Then the music of the sea rises. In all three performances the Sultan's theme is loudest, and they differ in **how big they build the later part**.

The first Promenade in Ravel's orchestration: a solo trumpet states the walking theme and the brass answer in chords. The give-and-take of the original piano piece becomes a contrast between solo and ensemble, and the sound broadens as strings and woodwinds join. In all three performances the last chord is loudest, and they differ in **whether the music rises once to nearly full volume in the middle**.

A tone poem in which a witches' night-long revel scatters at the sound of the dawn bells. Furious swirling strings and a heavy brass theme rush on until the bell tolls, and then clarinet and flute sing of a quiet dawn. All three performances reduce the sound after the bell, and they differ in **how softly they play the dawn section**.

The orchestral introduction of the first movement, in which the clarinet softly states the first theme in B minor. The theme begins quietly over low strings, swells gradually, bursts into a big full-orchestra tutti, and then fades again. Since the cello has not yet entered, the differences among the three performances are the conductor's, and **how long they sustain the big tutti** differs most.

The opening of the F major first movement: over the gentle tremolo of the two violins and a low sustained note in the cello, the viola brings in the first theme. The first violin soon takes up the plain pentatonic melody, and all four instruments grow together. Two performances reach the climax within 30 seconds, while **only one postpones its climax to the middle**.

The opening of the second movement, where the English horn sings the first theme after slow wind chords. The chords begin softly, rise up loudly once and then subside, while muted strings support the melody from below. In all three performances the chords are the loudest part, and they differ in **how softly they play the melody section**.

The complete Humoresque No. 7, whose dotted-rhythm melody sways lightly in G♭ major. In the middle a minor-key shadow falls and the volume swells; then the first melody returns and ends quietly. All three performances are loudest at the same spot, and their lengths vary **from 2:33 to 2:57**.

The opening, where a solo horn calls out the theme over very softly trembling strings. The winds take up the call one by one and the sound builds, and at the end the whole orchestra rises up loudly. The long crescendo is the same in all three performances, and they differ in **how quietly they hold back the opening**.

A short votive piece in C major for unaccompanied four-part chorus (Locus iste). The first line, “This place was made by God,” spreads out in broad chords, and in the middle the harmony passes through several keys and subsides softly. Two performances are loudest early on, while **only one puts its loudest sound later**.

A funeral march that begins with a triplet signal played by a solo trumpet. The signal swells into a cry from the whole orchestra and then subsides, after which the strings take up the C-sharp minor march theme and walk on heavily. All three performances come close to full volume after about 25 seconds, and they differ in **how long they draw out that cry**.

The opening of the “Resurrection,” where cellos and double basses charge fiercely upward over wild string tremolos. The C minor theme that follows walks as heavily as a funeral march. In all three performances the music sinks at the same spot and is loudest at the end. They differ in **how deeply they let the middle sink**.

The “Titan” opens with the whole string section sustaining a single A, very softly. Over this ground, which the score marks “Wie ein Naturlaut” (like a sound of nature), a descending fourth motif in the woodwinds and a distant trumpet signal emerge one by one. **How early they reach nearly full volume** is where the three performances differ most.

The passage that opens with two choirs crying out “Veni, creator spiritus” (Come, Creator Spirit) over an E♭ major organ chord. The two choruses trade the same words, while orchestra and brass fill in above them together. **How loudly they come in from the very first cry** is where the three performances differ most.

The first song of Das Lied von der Erde opens with a violently rising horn signal, and soon the tenor begins a song offering a cup of wine. The text is a German rendering of a poem by Li Bai, so the darkness of life shows through the exuberant drinking song. In each of the three performances, **the loudest sound falls in a different place: the opening, the middle, or the end**.

The introduction before the waltz begins: over soft string tremolo, the horn plays a rising motif. The introduction rises loudly a few times and subsides to catch its breath, and the first waltz in D major then begins by turning that motif into a dance melody. The performances differ from **the loudness of the first tremolo** onward.

Franck's Violin Sonata opens the way with a soft piano chord. The violin sings gently with a short rising-and-falling motif, which returns again and again in the later movements in changing forms. All three performances begin softly and go to their loudest at the end. Each sets **the loudness of the first sound** differently.

A short prayer for solo soprano, the Pie Jesu. Where other requiems spread out the song of judgment on a large scale, Fauré left only the prayer at its end. Each time a vocal line ends, the accompaniment answers briefly and carries on. The three performances differ on **whether the loudest line comes early or late**.

A song in which the singer flies up toward the light with a beloved in a dream, then wakes and calls the night back. Over the piano's evenly repeated chords, the voice spins long lines. In the last stanza the dream breaks, and the song pleads for the night to return. **The duration** ranges from 2:40 to 3:20.

A slow dance, the Pavane: plucked strings mark the steps and the flute brings in the F-sharp minor melody. The melody passes through several instruments, and around the middle comes a passage where the whole orchestra sounds heavily. All three performances swell in the middle, and they differ in **whether they sink deeply once within the loud passage**.

A siciliana in which the cello sings a G minor melody over a slowly rocking dance rhythm. The piano opens first with that rhythm; the cello takes up the melody, goes around once, spreads into a new section, and returns to the first melody. The three performances follow nearly the same course, and they differ in **length and where they sing loudest**.

The opening of the first movement of Clara Schumann's only piano trio. The violin sings the G minor theme from the very first note, and soon all three instruments climb forcefully together. All three performances are loudest at around the 30-second mark, and they differ in **how evenly they carry on after that**.

The opening of the first movement of the symphony Bizet wrote at seventeen. It opens with a forceful chord from the whole orchestra, and the strings bring out a first theme that soars on a C major chord. Forceful tutti and light string steps alternate. The performances differ on whether **the loudest point** comes early or late.

The opening of the piano concerto Clara Schumann wrote as a teenager. The orchestral tutti proudly sounds the first A minor chord to open the movement, then the sound soon settles down and the theme follows. All three open loudly and sink deeply later, and they differ on **whether the loudest sound is placed at the opening or later**.

The first of Clara Schumann's three romances, a slow song in D♭ major. The piano opens briefly and the violin takes up a long melody, swelling and subsiding several times as the song continues. All three performances are loudest at the same spot, and they differ in **how deeply they let the later soft passage sink**.

The first two minutes or so of the first-movement introduction, where the orchestra lays out the theme at length first. After a forceful opening chord it drops straight to soft playing, and loud surges and hushed moments alternate in short stretches. All three performances share this shape, and they differ on **whether the strongest sound falls on the first chord or in the surging passage about a minute in**.

The opening of the rondo that contains the La campanella (“little bell”) theme Liszt later arranged for piano. A small bell chimes in between statements of the theme, and the solo violin and orchestra trade the B minor theme. The flow is the same in all three performances, and they differ in **how far they come down after the loudest point**.

A piece named after Clementi's collection of studies, teasing a child practicing the piano. Right-hand sixteenth notes roll on without rest, slow down and soften in the middle, roll on again and close forcefully. **How long and how deeply the middle sinks** is where the three performances differ most.

The first scene, of day breaking over the sea. Over soft timpani tremolo and low strings the harp draws a figure, and the English horn and a muted trumpet together offer a short melody. The sound, begun very slowly (Très lent), wakes bit by bit. Performances differ in **how quietly the first sound is played**.

The piece opens with an unaccompanied flute theme that slides down by semitones and returns. Harp and horns soon answer quietly, and the flute theme comes back over changing harmonies below. All three performances are loudest at the end, and they differ in **how deeply they let the early part sink**.

A prelude in which a singing middle section sits between outer sections of short, bouncing march-rhythm chords. In the middle the tempo eases a little (Un poco meno mosso) and a long melody flows over the left-hand accompaniment. Performances differ in **how deeply the middle song is allowed to sink**.

The variation in which the solo piano turns the Paganini theme upside down into a slow song in D♭ major. The orchestra takes up the melody the piano gave first, rises up loudly, and sinks to a soft close at the end. The flow is the same in all three performances, and they differ in **when the climax comes and how long it is sustained**.

A single whip crack, and the piccolo plays a lively first theme to open the movement. The trumpet takes up the theme and the whole orchestra climbs high, and then the sound drops sharply and moves to a relaxed, jazz-tinged melody. All three performances are loudest within the first 25 seconds, and they differ in **how deeply the relaxed passage is allowed to sink**.

The opening, where the snare drum begins to etch out the same rhythm very softly. Over pizzicato violas and cellos the flute brings out the first theme, and then the clarinet takes up the same theme. All three performances are loudest at the end, and they differ in **when they reach nearly full volume**.

A piano piece in which the right hand sings a slow melody over broken chords spread evenly by the left hand. The tempo mark is “without slowness” (Andantino sans lenteur), so although it is dreamlike, it never stops flowing. All three performances are loudest at the same spot, and they differ in **how softly the first melody is brought out**.

A song lamenting the wounds Fortune has dealt (Fortune plango vulnera), repeating the same music for three stanzas. In each stanza the chorus begins softly and rises with the orchestra to close it. All three performances end the three stanzas similarly loud, and the difference lies in **how softly they sink back when a new stanza begins**.

Satie's slow waltz, an adaptation for solo piano of a song written for a cabaret singer. The left hand marks the waltz accompaniment with a bass on the first beat and chords on the other two, and the right hand takes the song melody. **The length** differs greatly from performance to performance: one is a minute longer than the other two.

The chorus invoking the goddess Fortune that opens and closes the entire work. It begins with heavy cries from the chorus and timpani, then the chorus repeats the same rhythm very softly before bursting out in the last verse and driving to the end. All three performances follow the same course, and they differ on **whether the loudest sound is the first cry or the last**.

The opening of Ravel's piece imitating Hungarian Gypsy music: a cadenza with which the violin begins alone, without accompaniment. It starts slowly (Lento), drawing the melody out on the low G string, and moves between hesitation and rushing, free of the beat. All three performances pause deeply once in the middle, and they differ on **whether the strongest sound comes before or after that pause**.

The first two minutes or so of the “Emerson” movement, where thick chords surge, subside for a while, and rise again. Ives wrote much of this movement without bar lines, leaving the flow largely to the performer. **How deeply the middle is allowed to sink** is where the three performances differ most.

A short prelude that poses a question to the entire symphony. Low strings open solemnly, and then the chorus sings the hymn “Watchman, tell us of the night.” The words are a dialogue between a night traveler and the watchman. All three performances are loudest about two-thirds of the way through, and **the same passage differs in length by nearly 40 seconds**.

At the opening of the War Requiem, over bells and low strings, the chorus intones “Requiem aeternam” (eternal rest) in low voices. The bells ring uneasily, repeating C and F-sharp, a tritone apart. All three performances sustain the soft passage for a long time and rise loudly at the end, and the only difference is **how long they draw out that soft passage**.

The opening, where the full orchestra states Purcell's theme all at once with force. Then woodwinds, brass, strings and percussion take up the same theme in turn, and finally everyone comes together again. **Whether the first or the last full-orchestra statement is played loudest** is where the three performances differ.

The suite opens with a slow, broad song for a single cello. This song (Canto) returns three more times in changed form between the movements. **Whether the loudest sound is placed early or at the end** is where the three performances differ most.

The first movement, which Berg wrote using the twelve-tone technique. As its name suggests, it moves in a jovial way (gioviale) and lasts around three minutes; it opens with a chord sounded by all four instruments and trades short motifs among them. All three performances are loudest at about one minute, and they differ in **how deeply they let the music sink after the climax**.

The opening of the concerto Berg wrote in memory of Manon Gropius, who died at eighteen. The clarinet and harp offer a soft figure, and the solo violin answers by touching its four open strings (G, D, A, E) in turn. Performances differ in **where the music rises highest**.

The complete first piece, which portrays the monument to Colonel Shaw, who led a Black regiment in the Civil War. Over very soft strings a slow march drags on as if shuffling its feet, with fragments of old songs mixed in faintly. It surges loudly once about two-thirds of the way through and then returns to the opening stillness. Performances differ in **how quietly the opening is kept**.

True to the instruction “violently moving” (Heftig bewegt), this movement alternates fierce shouts and hushed whispers again and again in under three minutes. Plucked and bowed sounds interleave in short fragments. All three performances shout out loudest near the end, but **the loudness of the whispers** varies from performance to performance.

The first movement of Webern's Symphony, a double canon in which the four voices are paired off and follow each other in inversion. The melody never stays long with one instrument but hops among horn, clarinet, harp and strings, one or two notes at a time. All three performances are loudest a little past the middle, and they differ in **how softly they play the beginning and the end**.

The movement that first presents the two themes running through the whole symphony. The heavy “statue theme” (thème-statue) played by trombones confronts the flower theme played softly by two clarinets, and after the piano cadenza several layers of rhythm pile up on top of each other at once. The three performances differ on **when they first play loudly**.

The first piece, depicting birds awakening at dawn. The clarinet takes the blackbird's song and the violin the nightingale's, while underneath the piano and cello tirelessly repeat fixed rhythms and chords. All three performances sound loudest about three-quarters of the way through, and they differ in **how softly they play before that**.

The Sabre Dance from the ballet Gayane. Over a relentlessly pounding rhythm the xylophone races through a sharp theme, and in the middle the saxophone and low strings sing a relaxed melody at length. Then the first theme returns and drives to the end. Performances differ in **how far the dynamic level drops in the middle song**.

The first movement opens fast and resolutely (Allegro con fermezza). The orchestra opens with a forceful tutti, and the solo violin soon enters and leads the first theme, with its clear rhythm. All three performances come close to full volume within 10 seconds, and they differ on **whether the loudest sound is in the first tutti or later**.

The waltz that opens the Masquerade Suite. Over a whirling accompaniment the violins spread out a wistful minor-key melody at full volume; the same theme returns several times and ends with the biggest surge at the very end. The flow is almost the same in all three performances, and they differ in **how long they sustain loud playing**.

Piazzolla's tango arranged three ways, for **cello, trumpet and string quartet**. The underlying repeated rhythm stays the same, and only the melody instrument changes. Lengths vary widely, from 3 minutes to 6 and a half, and only the cello version comes in loudly from the start.

You hear the same melody played by cello and orchestra, cello and piano, and violin and string ensemble. Only the cello-and-piano version is notated a whole tone lower, so that the cello sounds fuller. As for length, **the violin and string ensemble version is about a minute longer**.

Piazzolla's “Summer” in three instrumentations: **violin with string ensemble, string quartet with orchestra, and solo guitar**. The guitar version is shortest at 4:41, and the quartet-with-orchestra version is longest at 7:07.

All three sing it in A major, the key originally written for the tenor. The first verse is nearly the same, and the settings diverge in the second verse. In the Grigolo version the orchestra takes over, in the Domingo version the Vienna Boys' Choir joins, and in the Carreras version there is a duet with a boy soprano. **The Domingo version runs about 45 seconds longer**, so the lengths also differ greatly.

Piazzolla wrote this after losing his father. You hear the same piece in **violin, bandoneon with chorus, and two-piano** versions. Lengths range from 4:38 to 8:37, and the point of the highest peak varies from early on to near the end.
Being a wordless song sung on a single vowel, it can be performed by any instrument. Rachmaninoff himself also left an orchestral version. You hear the same melody in **voice, cello and orchestra**.

The passage that ends Act I, where Violetta shrugs off love as a vain dream and vows to live free. After the “Follie!” recitative, the fast cabaletta continues with dazzling ornamentation, and in the midst of it Alfredo's love song from outside the window breaks in. The three performances differ most in **whether they save the loudest sound until the very end**.

The opening of the Adagietto, played very slowly by strings and harp alone. Over the harp's arpeggios the first violins sing the theme very softly, and then the cellos take up the melody. At the cello entry Mahler wrote “do not drag.” **How slowly they draw it out** is where the three performances differ most, from 1:44 to 2:01.

The passage in which the piano alone opens the concerto with eight bars of bell-like chords. The chords begin softly and pile up, growing louder; then violins and violas and the clarinet bring in the first theme in C minor, while the piano fills in beneath with fast arpeggios. **How slowly the eight bells are tolled** is where the three performances differ most.

The start of the slow second movement of the “Emperor” Concerto. The strings, led by muted violins, sing a hymn in B major softly and surge up loudly twice; when they subside again, the piano enters very softly, descending from a high note. **How slowly the strings' hymn is drawn out** is where they differ most, from 1:48 to 2:01.

The opening of the second movement, where timpani cut in alone on the strings' octave motif. A fugato in which the strings enter softly, one every four bars, swells at length and bursts into a fortissimo of the full orchestra; after the woodwinds briefly catch their breath, the second theme in C major returns, again in fortissimo. The performances differ in **which of the two fortissimos they give more weight**.

A scene in which Violetta, writing a farewell letter, hides it from Alfredo, cries “Love me, Alfredo,” and leaves. The first part is a dialogue of short exchanges, and at the end the melody of the Act I prelude bursts out. **The length of the whole scene** is where the three performances differ most, from 2:06 to 2:40.

The passage at the end of the fourth movement's march section where chorus and full orchestra sing the first verse of the “Ode to Joy” together in D major. The melody carries on the march's 6/8 meter and ends just before the slow “Seid umschlungen” begins. All three performances are loudest at the very first sound, and they differ in **whether they climb back up to that level in the big passage that follows**.

The complete overture to The Marriage of Figaro, in which soft whispers of strings and bassoons and loud full-orchestra sound collide without pause. There is no development: from a short string link at the end of the exposition it moves straight into the recapitulation. Mozart originally meant to put a slow movement here, but dropped it and joined the two halves with this link. **How deeply the soft passages are lowered** is where the three performances differ most.

The aria that opens the Goldberg Variations, a sarabande in G major with a melody densely hung with ornaments. The 32 bars are divided into two halves of 16 bars, each repeated, and the bass of this aria forms the skeleton of the 30 variations that follow. All three performances observe every repeat, and the biggest difference is in **whether they lower the dynamics on repeating**.

The passage in which the men's chorus shouts fiercely at the damned and the women's chorus softly pleads “call me.” After this confrontation goes back and forth twice, all four voices together prostrate themselves in prayer, moving from A minor to A♭ minor, a semitone lower, and the last chord leads into the Lacrimosa. **How quietly the women's chorus passages are played** is where the three performances differ most.

All three performances play Rameau's complete harpsichord piece “Tambourin” in E minor on the piano, as in the film The Handmaiden. The left hand sounds E and B together to imitate a drum, and above it the right hand's fast refrain keeps returning. **Only Hewitt plays the first refrain once more.** Beyond that, tempo differs most, so the lengths range from 1:08 to 1:27.

The G major prelude that opens the first of the unaccompanied cello suites. Broken chords flow without pause, stop once at a fermata on a high D in the very middle, and the second half sounds the open D string repeatedly over a long semitone-by-semitone ascent before closing in G major. **How deeply the soft passages are allowed to sink** is where the three performances differ most.

The C major prelude that opens Book I of the Well-Tempered Clavier. A broken-chord figure runs through nearly all of its 35 bars; in the second half a long G in the bass builds tension before it closes with a single C major chord over a C in the bass. **How slowly the same figure is traced** is where the three performances differ most, from 1:44 to 2:22.

The complete E minor étude nicknamed the “wrong note” étude. In the fast outer sections, grace notes that clash with the melody by a semitone run throughout, giving a playful feel; the middle changes to E major, Più lento, with the left hand singing a long melody and the right hand wrapping it in wide broken chords. **How leisurely the same score is drawn out** is where the three performances differ most, from 2:50 to 3:24.

Cavaradossi's Act III aria, sung before his execution as he remembers the nights he loved. A solo clarinet first presents the melody in B minor, and the tenor, from “O dolci baci,” takes it up almost unchanged and drives on to “muoio disperato.” **Whether the first climax is sung as loudly as the last** is where the three performances differ most.

The chorale “Jesus bleibet meine Freude,” the tenth movement that closes Cantata BWV 147. The orchestra keeps up a melody flowing in triplets without pause, and between them the chorus inserts the hymn tune line by line. **How loudly they raise the volume on each line where the chorus enters** is where the three performances differ most.

The first movement of “Winter,” to which Vivaldi attached a sonnet, depicting shivering in the cold amid snow. From the lowest strings, voice after voice piles up repeating the same note, and trills are laid on top; then the solo violin storms alone in fast figures like a biting wind. **How long the soft introduction is drawn out before the first big rise** is where the three performances differ, from about 25 seconds to over 40.

The “Hallelujah” chorus that closes Part II of Messiah. In this D major chorus with added trumpets and timpani, the four voices sing “The kingdom of this world” together like a hymn in the middle, and at “King of Kings” the sopranos and trumpet cry out on one note and climb higher and higher. **How low the soft middle passage is brought** is where the three performances differ most.

The passage where Elgar's Cello Concerto begins with a recitative for solo cello. The cello strikes chords forcefully, nobilmente, and the clarinets, bassoons and horns answer briefly; then the violas present the 9/8 Moderato theme first and the cello takes it up. **How deep the soft spot in the middle of the introduction is** is where the three performances differ most.

The passage that opens the finale of the “New World.” The strings repeat a two-note semitone rise, growing denser and louder, then horns and trumpets state the E minor theme loudly while the other instruments support with short chords. After the theme is repeated once more, the violins take it up. **How much quieter the strings' opening is than the brass theme** is where the three performances differ most.

The complete A minor étude nicknamed “Winter Wind.” Four slow (Lento) bars first present the theme softly, and once the fast section (Allegro con brio) begins, the right hand plays a ceaselessly cascading figure while the left hand carries that theme heavily. **The overall length** differs most among the three performances, from 3:22 to 3:55, and so does where the loudest sound is placed.

The passage in which the Adagietto builds to its last big climax and ends. The strings grow gradually louder until they reach a very loud (ff) spot where the harp strikes an F major chord forcefully, then come down “slowing greatly” and disappear on the quietest (pppp) chord. **How much these fourteen bars are stretched** is where the three performances differ most, from 1:18 to 1:55.

The fast march that closes the William Tell Overture (Allegro vivace). After a trumpet fanfare, the strings open a galloping-rhythm theme softly and the whole orchestra answers very loudly; in the middle, bassoons and horns lay very soft, gentle long notes over fast violin figures. **How deeply this middle section is lowered** is where the three performances differ most, and so is how loudly the last minute is pushed.

The complete first movement of Shostakovich's Piano Concerto No. 2. The bassoon first states the theme and the piano answers with single notes spread in octaves between the hands; in the middle a new D minor theme gradually fades, and then the orchestra suddenly bursts out loudly. After the big climax, the piano plays a fugato alone. **How much the D minor passage and the piano solo passage are lowered** is where the three performances differ most.

The complete F# major barcarolle: over a left hand rocking in 12/8, the right hand sings in thirds and sixths. The middle moves to A major and begins softly (sotto voce); at the end the F# major theme returns loudly (f), swells to very loud (ff), passes through a soft fast figure, and closes very loudly. **Whether the loud passage of the early theme is played as loudly as the ending** is where the three performances differ most.

Liszt's arrangement for solo piano of Schumann's song “Widmung” (“Dedication”), in A♭ major. In the middle E major section, the right hand repeats triplet chords softly, and later those triplet chords return in A♭ major to support the melody at fortississimo (fff). **How leisurely it unfolds** is where the three performances differ most, from 3:29 to 3:55.

The opening of the funeral march, the third movement of Chopin's Sonata No. 2. The left hand alternates chords of B♭ and G♭ major like tolling bells, and above it the melody, repeating the single note B♭, walks softly (p) before moving to a passage piling up loud (f) chords. **How low the soft steps are held before the loud chords** is where the three performances differ most, and the lengths also range from 1:13 to 1:31.

Rachmaninoff's solo piano arrangement of Kreisler's “Liebesleid.” It starts as a waltz in A minor, passes through a faster section that turns to A major, and after a very loud (ff) climax goes through a soft fast figure and closes in A major. **How deeply the soft passage after the climax is lowered** is where the three performances differ most, and the lengths also range from 4:11 to 4:50.

The complete C major étude, the first of Chopin's Op. 10. The right hand runs up and down sixteenth-note broken chords built on tenths through as many as six octaves without pause, and the left hand supports with a slow melody in octaves. The score says f throughout and never rises to ff, so **where the loudest sound is placed** is where the three performances differ most.

The complete slow movement in F major made widely known by the film Elvira Madigan. Muted strings first play the whole theme over a triplet accompaniment and pizzicato, and then the piano enters and sings the same melody. **How slowly it is drawn out** is where the three performances differ most, from 6:08 to 7:04.

The complete B♭ minor Adagio, which Barber arranged for string orchestra from the slow movement of his string quartet. The melody moving stepwise up and down piles up higher and higher and reaches its climax on four big chords; after a long rest the first melody returns and fades on an unresolved chord. **How slowly it is drawn out** is where they differ most, from 7:23 to 8:33.

The opening of the first movement of Symphony No. 25, heard at the start of the film Amadeus. The strings state the G minor syncopated theme loudly and repeat it once, then the oboe touches the notes of that theme softly in long notes, and as the music turns to B♭ major the string tremolo surges again loudly. **Whether the repeat of the theme is also pushed loudly** is where the three performances differ most.

The complete third movement of the Gran Partita, in which Salieri in Amadeus marvels as he points to the oboe and clarinet. Over an E♭ major accompaniment in which the winds repeat notes like a pulse, the oboe sustains one long note and the clarinet takes it up, and then three instruments, including the basset horn, trade the melody. **How slowly it is drawn out** is where they differ most, from 4:57 to 5:50.

The fifth piece, closing the Mother Goose Suite, a C major piece marked slow and solemn (Lent et grave). It opens with soft strings, sings quietly for a long time, and closes loudly with glissandos in the last bars. **How long the final loud passage is held loud** is where the three performances differ most.

The instrumental sonatina that opens a cantata written for a funeral. Very slowly (Molto adagio), two recorders echo each other, supported below by two violas da gamba and the continuo. **Whether the sound fills out loudly from the start or opens softly and grows toward the middle** is where the three performances differ most.

An aria in C minor based on Simeon's song as he holds the infant Jesus in his arms, singing “I have enough; I would gladly depart even today.” The oboe first brings out a melody leaping up a minor sixth, and the solo voice takes it up and sings “Ich habe genug.” **How slowly it is sung** is where the three performances differ most, from 6:45 to 8:07.

April from The Seasons, a B♭ major piece depicting the spring flower the snowdrop. A poem by Maykov is printed at the head of the score, the marking “un poco rubato” is given, and there is a D minor section in the middle. **How deeply and long the soft passage is held** is where the three performances differ most.

Solveig's song from Act IV, which she sings in front of the hut while waiting for Peer Gynt. The strings open the prelude in unison, and after two rounds of the A minor verse (Un poco Andante) and the wordless A major dance-like section (Allegretto tranquillamente), the strings close again. **How slowly it is carried along** is where the three performances differ most, from 4:46 to 5:52.

The passage in the slow second movement of Mendelssohn's Violin Concerto (Andante, C major) where the solo violin sings the first theme. A long melody resembling the composer's own piano collection Songs Without Words continues and ends just before the dark A minor middle section. **How slowly it is sung** is where the three performances differ most, from 2:45 to 3:19.

The opening of Saint-Saëns's Danse Macabre, where the harp strikes D twelve times to mark midnight. The solo violin, with its E string tuned down to E♭, draws a tritone, and after the flute's waltz theme and the violin's descending second theme, the whole orchestra sounds the waltz loudly. **Whether the big climb 30 seconds before the end is made in one go or in two stages** is where they differ most.

The slow first part (Andante, E major) of Rosina's cavatina “Una voce poco fa,” which she sings holding a letter. After the orchestral prelude the song of confessing love follows, and the forceful vow “Sì, Lindoro mio sarà” appears twice, before and after. In all three, a mezzo-soprano sings in the key Rossini wrote. **How long the same passage is sung** is where the three performances differ most, from 2:10 to 2:35.

The passage in the second movement (B major) of the “Emperor” Concerto where the strings' hymn ends and the piano enters for the first time. The piano comes in softly, descending from a high note, and continues the song; in all three performances it grows louder toward the end. It includes only what was heard in the film, so it ends mid-phrase. **How slowly the same passage is unfolded** is where they differ most, from 48 to 58 seconds.

The passage where the finale of Chopin's Piano Concerto No. 1, the Rondo (Vivace, E major), begins. After a brief orchestral opening, the piano presents the rondo theme for the first time, in the rhythm of the Polish dance known as the krakowiak. **Whether the last phrase of the theme is built back up to close** is where the three performances differ most.

The complete work for violin and orchestra that Saint-Saëns dedicated to Sarasate. Over plucked strings the violin sings a slow, melancholy introduction (Andante malinconico); in the fast rondo the orchestra-only tuttis break in loudly twice, and the ending turns to A major and closes faster (Più allegro). **Whether the loudest sound comes in an early tutti or the final chord** is where the three performances differ most.

About the first three minutes of the fourth movement, in which Mahler set the “Midnight Song” from Nietzsche's Zarathustra. Over muted cellos and basses alternating between two notes, the alto sings “O Mensch! Gib Acht!” (O man! Take heed!), and the oboe draws notes upward “like a sound of nature.” The score marks the whole passage “very soft throughout” from the start. **Which phrase carries the loudest sound** is where the three performances differ most.

The Venusberg dance that opens Act I of Wagner's Tannhäuser. Bacchantes break roughly into the nymphs' dance, and when the sirens sing “Naht euch dem Strande” (Come to the shore), the dance answers more wildly and subsides at the end. All three use the Dresden version, before it was greatly expanded for Paris, and **how fast they drive it** is where they differ most, from 4:29 to 5:00.

The Act II finale scene in which the statue of the Commendatore accepts the supper invitation and visits Don Giovanni. The chords that opened the overture turn into a diminished seventh and sound louder (ff) than in the overture as the statue enters; Don Giovanni, refusing to the end to repent, is dragged to hell in the Allegro amid a chorus from beneath the earth. **How slowly it is drawn out** is where the three performances differ most, from 6:31 to 8:01.

The first two minutes of the last symphony Mahler completed. Cellos and horns touch A in alternation and the harp sounds a four-note motif, then the second violins trade a D major theme falling two notes at a time with the horn. At the end it turns to D minor and brass and timpani enter loudly. **How slowly the D major opening is drawn out** is where the three performances differ most, from 2:01 to 2:22.

The opening of the overture to Wagner's opera about the cursed sailor condemned to wander the sea. Over strings storming like a tempest, horns and bassoons blow the Dutchman motif loudly; the whole orchestra strikes twice, at ff and fff, then gradually softens and halts on a rest. **How big the build is from the first f to the ff** is where the three performances differ most.

The slow opening of the overture to Wagner's early opera Rienzi. The trumpet swells and fades on a long A, sending a signal three times, and the strings answer softly each time; after a passage rising by semitones, the strings sing the melody of Rienzi's Prayer from Act V all the way through for the first time. **How loud the trumpet signals sound** is where the three performances differ most.

The opening of the last symphony Bruckner never finished. Over a soft D tremolo in the strings, eight horns sound the introductory theme; the horns rise loudly, moving the harmony far afield, then subside, and the passage ends as the music begins to build again. **How quickly the introduction is moved along** is where the three performances differ most, from 1:45 to 2:06.

The 3/8 Allegro that closes Vivaldi's Bassoon Concerto in E minor. The tutti plays the ritornello four times, and in the solo passages between them the strings mostly rest while the bassoon continues its fast figures with the continuo. Lengths range from 2:50 to 3:19, and most of that difference comes from **the length of the final tutti**.

The slow introduction (Adagio sostenuto) that opens the first movement of the Kreutzer Sonata, and the first theme of the Presto. The violin alone opens with four bars on an A major chord, the piano answers and leans toward the minor, and after stopping very softly, the piano echoes the theme the violin brings in at the A minor Presto. The ending bar is the same in all three, and **how slowly the introduction moves** is where they differ most, from 1:28 to 1:55.

The passage where the polonaise begins in Chopin's Andante spianato et Grande polonaise brillante. The orchestra sounds a signal in polonaise rhythm and rises in a crescendo to ff, then after a bar's rest and a soft slowing, the piano brings out the E♭ major theme a little more slowly (Meno mosso). **How low the orchestral crescendo starts** is where the three performances differ most.

The complete first movement of Mozart's Sonata for Two Pianos in D major. The two pianos begin by sounding the same melody forcefully in unison, then one takes up a phrase the other has brought out, and they share the themes. All three repeat the exposition, and **how deep the soft passages are** is where they differ most.

The complete first movement of Mozart's four-hand sonata in C major, played by two people sitting side by side at one piano. Primo and secondo bring out the theme forcefully in octave unison, and then trade delicate answers; all three repeat only the exposition. **Lengths range from 8:06 to 9:04**, and whether the loudest sound is placed at the start or at the end also varies.

The Adagio from the ballet, depicting Gayane's despair. It is played by strings alone and begins with a slow, smooth melody in the low register. **Lengths range from 4:22 to 5:06**, which is where the three performances differ most, and how deep the dips between the loud passages go also varies.

The Kyrie in which twenty voices, five parts each divided in four, layer semitone-moving melodies so densely that it is heard as a mass of sound rather than individual melodies. It is built as an enormous fugue, and the middle section where Christe is sung is much gentler. **How deep the soft middle passage is** is where the three performances differ most.

The first aria (Larghetto) of a shepherd weeping over the heartless Dorilla. To depict the word “weeping” (lagrimar), Vivaldi has the strings of the same part play partly pizzicato and partly with the bow. **How soft the pizzicato opening is** is where the three performances differ most.

Rodelinda's Act II aria, in which she, having promised to marry Grimoaldo only if he kills her son with his own hands, defies him with “Spietati” (merciless ones). In the middle she sings that she can never join hands with that cruel man, then returns to the first part. **The length, from 4:13 to 4:51**, is where the three performances differ most.

The first 44 bars of the “Eroica” first movement. The whole orchestra strikes an E♭ chord twice loudly (f), then the cellos bring out the theme softly (p), and in the seventh bar it veers off to C♯. With repeated sf accents, the whole orchestra sounds the theme very loudly (ff) at bar 37. **The tempo at which the same 44 bars pass, in 47 to 52 seconds**, is where the three performances differ most.

A piece in which a 16-part chorus sings, without accompaniment, the “eternal light” phrase of the requiem mass. The women's chorus starts on a single F and widens the pitches, in the middle the sopranos enter clearly on G and the chorus spreads over more than two octaves, and later the sopranos and tenors touch B, the highest note of the piece. The score has no marking louder than p, and **how deep the later soft passage is** is where the three performances differ most.

Halvorsen's rewrite for string duo of the Passacaglia, the last piece of Handel's harpsichord Suite No. 7 (G minor). It was originally for violin and viola, but all three performances use violin and cello. Over a four-bar theme it varies with changing techniques such as pizzicato and ponticello and closes on a G major chord. **How deep the soft middle passage is** is where the three performances differ most.

The slow introduction of a symphonic scherzo that follows Goethe's ballad. Over muted strings the clarinet first presents the broom theme, the music suddenly races ahead, and after a single timpani stroke and a long rest, the bassoon plays that theme through to the end for the first time. **Whether the racing passage is played at full strength right away or builds toward the end** is where the three performances differ most.

Rodelinda's last aria in Handel's opera Rodelinda. At the end of the opera she sings of her joy and love at being reunited with her husband Bertarido. All three performances come close to full volume once early on, and **how long and deep the soft passage that follows is** is where they differ most.

From the return of the closing theme in C minor at the end of the first movement's recapitulation to the stop on the diminished-seventh fermata. The closing theme, which starts softly (p) and rises to f, appears twice; after the rising figure of the first theme returns, a very loud (ff) diminished seventh is held at length. **How long the final diminished seventh is held** is where the three performances differ most.

The introduction that opens the tone poem, “Sunrise.” Over a low C held by organ, contrabassoon and double basses, the trumpet plays a rising C–G–C motif, and the harmony shifts between major and minor before closing loudly in C major with the organ added. **How much time they take to reach the final C major** is where the three performances differ most, and the lengths range from 1:38 to 1:57.
